definition: The last mile in the context of artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLM) is a metaphor drawing on last mile (telecommunications) to refers to the limit or "gap" of what an AI model "knows" and human knowledge.
details: Attending to the last mile gap is a strategy also to address algorithmic bias. The last mile concept was used prior to the public rollout of ChatGPT in 2022, and gained traction in 2024 from multiple sources simultaneously. and amplified by Forbes Magazine. The "last mile" concept in AI entered common use in 2025 to refer to algorithm gaps, AI design gaps, and other gaps.

explainer.lead: The last mile in AI is a metaphor for the gap between what a model knows and human knowledge. It matters because attending to this gap is also a strategy for addressing algorithmic bias.

tiers.eli5: It's the final stretch between what the AI can do and what people actually need it to do in real life.
tiers.practitioner: Teams treat closing the last mile as part of deployment, including bias mitigation, rather than assuming a trained model is finished. A pitfall is planning for the model and not for the remaining gap, where design and algorithm gaps surface.
tiers.paperLevel: The last mile, borrowed from telecommunications, refers to the limit or gap between model knowledge and human knowledge; the concept entered common use in 2025 to refer to algorithm gaps, AI design gaps and other gaps. It is a framing metaphor, not a formal measure.

explainer.example: A deployed model performs well in testing but fails on real users' needs; closing the last mile means addressing that gap and the associated bias before rollout.
